source_document.body:
Andalucía Trade’s Rosa de Leyva, Pelayo García and Beatriz Feichtenberger at the Critical Minerals Forum & Global Market Access event in Seville on Oct. 19. The organizers brought together Canadian and Andalusian mining representatives to explore investment and collaboration opportunities. Credit: C.McClelland
By: Colin McClelland in Seville October 19, 2026
The Andalucia region in Spain wants to attract mining investors with faster approvals and access to hundreds of areas covered by expired mineral rights, as Europe seeks the capacity to mine at least 10% of its annual consumption of strategic raw materials by 2030.
The southern region accounts for about 90% of the value of Spain’s metal mining and ranks second in the European Union for copper output, behind Poland, regional officials said Monday. Its producers include Atalaya Mining (LSE: ATYM), which operates the Cerro Colorado open pit in the Riotinto district of Huelva province.
“Last year we got the permitting of a new mine from the beginning in just 27 months,” Jesús Portillo García-Pintos, the region’s director-general for sustainable mining and raw materials science, told an international mining forum in Seville. “Twenty-seven months in the mining sector is a dream, we know.”
Andalucia’s pitch extends beyond opening mines: officials want investors to process more minerals locally, develop mining technology and create skilled jobs that help retain the region’s graduates. Faster permits and public funding are intended to turn its mineral wealth into a broader industrial base as Europe seeks to reduce its reliance on imported raw materials.
Targets
The EU’s mining capacity already covered about 8% of its strategic raw-material consumption when the targets were set, European auditors estimated in a 2026 report , using 2016–2020 data. That aggregate masks deeper shortfalls in materials such as natural graphite and rare earths.
Even with faster approvals, meeting Europe’s 2030 goals will be difficult, Portillo acknowledged when questioned about the timetable. Developing processing industries could be easier than opening new mines, he said, although both present challenges.
Andalucia had 73 active exploration permits as of August. It put more than 450 expired mining rights out to tender across its eight provinces in 2025, Portillo said. The region has nearly 480 active mines and quarries.
A dedicated government unit coordinates departments to accelerate project approvals. Investors can also consult geological maps, mineral-rights information and other technical material through the government’s mining portal .
Incentives
Andalucia has earmarked €40 million (C$63.2 million) in mining incentives covering innovation in exploration, mineral processing and waste treatment, alongside energy efficiency.
Improving geological knowledge of both deposits and historical mining waste is another priority, including through cooperation with Spain’s geological survey, Portillo said.
“We have to strengthen this knowledge, not only about the primary resources, but also the secondary resources, the wastes,” he said. “Andalucia has a substantial mining past so in the wastes, we have a big body that we can provide.”
Andalucia assumed leadership in January of S3P Mining Regions, a European Commission-backed partnership promoting innovation and cooperation among mining areas.
The partnership now spans seven countries following Poland’s addition in September, Portillo said. Alongside Spain, the other participants are Finland, Sweden, France, Portugal and Greece. Cooperation connects regions with strong mining operations to those with more developed processing industries and technology.
Mines, processing
Much of Andalucia’s metal mining is concentrated in the Iberian Pyrite Belt, which extends across southwestern Spain into Portugal. Existing plants, ports and engineering suppliers provide infrastructure for further development.
Atalaya’s Riotinto plant can process 15 million tonnes annually. The company aims to use it as a regional processing hub, with Masa Valverde, San Dionisio and San Antonio among its surrounding deposits.
Sandfire Resources (ASX: SFR) owns the MATSA complex , also in Huelva. Its Aguas Teñidas, Magdalena and Sotiel underground mines feed a central plant with annual capacity of 4.7 million tonnes, producing copper and zinc concentrates with lead and silver byproducts.
The EU’s ambitions extend downstream, with 2030 benchmarks for domestic capacity to process 40% and recycle 25% of the union’s annual strategic raw-material consumption.
Near Seville, Cobre Las Cruces illustrates the processing investment officials want to attract. Global Panduro, controlled by Resource Capital Funds, acquired the business from First Quantum Minerals (TSX: FM) in June.
The new owner is advancing an underground mine and refinery designed to produce copper, zinc, lead and silver. The European Commission designated the development a strategic project in March 2025 under its critical raw materials act.
Atlantic Copper, owned by Freeport-McMoRan (NYSE: FCX), inaugurated its CirCular plant in Huelva in September. It is designed to process up to 60,000 tonnes of electrical and electronic equipment annually, recovering copper and other metals.
Training for growth
The region’s education system is another draw for investors, said Elena Gallego, head of the Invest in Andalucía department at regional business agency Andalucía Trade.
Andalucia has 15 universities educating about 250,000 students and roughly 900 vocational training centres, according to figures presented at the forum and published by Spain’s investment promotion agency.
Universities and vocational centres work with companies to tailor training to their equipment, technologies and staffing needs, Gallego said. Her investment service helps companies select sites, find staff and establish operations.
“We have always been a net exporter of talent in the region,” she said. “We did not have enough opportunities for all the professionals coming out of these universities to stay in the region.” Attracting investment could help bring some of those workers home, she added.
Manuel Sevilla Ramos, director of the Centre of Excellence and Innovation for Sustainable Mining, an initiative of Spanish metal mining association Aminer, said the opportunity extends beyond extraction.
“The real challenge is to build around our resources a value chain capable of generating knowledge, innovation, jobs, technology, and industrial security,” he said.
The centre connects companies, universities and researchers on issues including water management, digitalization, safety and training.
Canadian connection
Canada’s Mining Innovation Commercialization Accelerator, or MICA , is exploring how Canadian technology suppliers could work with Spanish operators and how Spanish innovations could serve the projects it supports.
The federally funded C$45-million initiative, managed by the Sudbury-based Centre for Excellence in Mining Innovation, has funded 75 innovation projects and helped bring 24 technologies to mine-site pilots, said Lorelei Ratushniak, its director of mining relations.
Her presentation proposed a demonstration at an Iberian operation or a joint Canada–Spain mining challenge in 2027.
“I’m very excited to see some of the challenges and opportunities from colleagues that presented this morning, particularly around waste,” Ratushniak said. “That is a great opportunity as we have a lot of technologies within that area, and again, we focus across the entire mining life cycle.”
Portillo identified access to mine sites for testing new technologies as another gap the region needs to address.
For Andalucia, investment also depends on community confidence. The region’s mining history dating to the Phoenicians and Romans helps, but communication, honest dialogue and transparency remain essential, Portillo said.
“If you don’t have social acceptance, it’s impossible to do mining.”
